headline_marked: [[Google launches Gemini 3.8 Flash]] for agents and a Cyber twin for vulnerability hunting
headline: Google launches Gemini 3.8 Flash for agents and a Cyber twin for vulnerability hunting
summary: The new Flash model is designed for agentic tasks and software development, while its Cyber variant excels at vulnerability detection, matching frontier-level performance.
details: Google has announced two versions of its new Gemini 3.8 Flash model: a standard Flash for agentic tasks and software development, and Flash Cyber for vulnerability detection. This marks Google's third Flash release in six weeks. It offers significant improvements in software engineering and multi-step reasoning.

The standard 3.8 Flash model delivers significant leaps from 3.7 Flash across software engineering, agentic tasks, and multi-step reasoning. It outperformed many large frontier models on the DeepSWE coding benchmark at a far lower cost. The model supports a 1M-token input window and a 64K-token output limit.

Flash Cyber is Google’s "most capable" cybersecurity model, matching frontier-level performance in discovering and patching vulnerabilities at scale. It scored 86.2% on the CyberGym benchmark and 47.2% on CWE-Bench. Internally, it achieved over 70% success in discovering vulnerabilities across 20 programming languages.

3.8 Flash is available now in Gemini Enterprise and for developers via the Gemini API through Google AI Studio, Google Antigravity, or Android Studio. It can ingest text, images, audio, video, and PDF files. Users can customize model effort levels based on needs for quality, cost, and latency.

The model can build complex applications from simple prompts, such as a 3D game with puzzles and storytelling. It also created a fully-functional DOS version of Google Maps, an interactive 3D device visualizer, and a topographic map based on real datasets.

According to Arena.ai, 3.8 Flash landed at No. 14 in Agent Arena and debuted at No. 7 in Text Arena, ranking above models like DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Claude Opus 5. It significantly improved over Gemini 3.7 Flash in multi-turn requests, writing, coding, and instruction following.

Flash Cyber is being rolled out to "trusted defenders" through Google’s Fairwind Program. This program prioritizes government authorities, critical-infrastructure operators, and other partners seeking advanced cyber defense capabilities.

headline_marked: Uber launches [[London's first commercial robotaxi service]] with safety drivers
headline: Uber launches London's first commercial robotaxi service with safety drivers
summary: Uber has beaten Waymo to market in London with its new robotaxi service, utilizing Wayve's AI-powered autonomous driving technology. Safety drivers are present for the initial rollout.
details: Uber has officially launched London's first commercial robotaxi service, marking a significant milestone in autonomous ride-hailing outside of the US and China. The service utilizes autonomous driving technology developed by UK startup Wayve, with Ford Mustang Mach-Es as the initial fleet vehicles.

While the vehicles are equipped with Wayve's AV2.0 system, which learns and adapts to new environments without relying on HD maps or lidar, they will initially feature licensed safety drivers. These drivers will monitor the ride but will not control the vehicle, and Uber plans to phase them out in favor of fully driverless operations.

Wayve's AV2.0 system is designed to operate without traditional constraints like geofencing, aiming for greater scalability and adaptability. The system relies on cameras and radar, similar to Tesla's approach, and is built to be hardware-agnostic.

Customers in London can opt-in to potentially be paired with an autonomous vehicle when booking rides through UberX, Uber Comfort, or Uber Electric. Maintenance and servicing of the fleet will be handled by Uber in partnership with Otto Car, while Wayve manages the autonomous driving system.

This launch positions Uber to set the standard for robotaxi experiences in London, even as competitors like Waymo and Lyft (in partnership with Baidu) also plan to introduce their autonomous services in the city later this year.

Wayve, founded in 2017 by machine learning PhD students, recently raised $1.2 billion from investors including Uber, Nvidia, and Stellantis, highlighting the significant backing for its AI-driven approach to autonomous driving.
